Learning Objectives
Describe the classic presentation and intraoperative findings of intraoperative periprosthetic
fractures.
Discuss the risk factors for and prevention of intraoperative periprosthetic fractures.
Discuss the classification systems for and current treatment options for intraoperative
periprosthetic fractures.
Describe surgical approach considerations for extending incisions in the management of
intraoperative periprosthetic fractures.
Overview
Fracture in the femur or acetabulum that occurs during placement of a prosthesis

Increasing incidence of total hip arthroplasty (THA) and expected increased incidence of
periprosthetic fractures (PPF)

Overview
PPFs are defined as fractures that occur adjacent to an implant. In relation to a THA
implant, these fractures are within the acetabulum and femur. In the past several
decades, the demand for THA has increased, and current projections anticipate
exponential growth.1,2 Given the increased prevalence of primary THA procedures
performed, the net number of intraoperative and postoperative PPFs likely will follow
this trend. Implant design, patient factors, and surgical technique contribute to this rare
but important event.
Epidemiology
Acetabular fractures: 0.2% cemented, 0.4% noncemented
Femoral fracture incidence: 0.1% to 5.4% with primary hip implants
Cementless: Approximately 5%
Cemented: 0.1% to 1%

Epidemiology
Intraoperative acetabulum PPFs are relatively rare, with an incidence of 0.4% for
noncemented components and 0.2% for cemented components.3 Because these
fractures are rare, they may be missed if the surgeon does not pay close attention.
Acetabular fractures may be particularly difficult to detect unless protrusio is present or
if the acetabular component goes through the medial acetabular wall. Risk factors
associated with intraoperative PPFs fall into two major categories: prosthesis-related and
patient-related factors. Prosthesis-related risk factors include noncemented (press-fit)
implants, under-reaming by more than 2 mm, elliptical monoblock components, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Periprosthetic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000508
2/28

revision surgery.3,4 Patient-related risk factors include female sex, osteopenia,
osteoporosis, dysplasia, and Paget disease.3,4
Intraoperative femur PPFs are more common, with a reported incidence ranging from
0.1% to 5.4% with primary THAs and 3% to 20.9% with the revision THA.3 The rates vary
substantially depending on whether the femoral components are cemented or
noncemented. Cemented femoral components are associated with an intraoperative
fracture rate ranging from 0.1% to 1%, whereas noncemented femoral components are
associated with an intraoperative fracture rate of approximately 5%.5 Risk factors for
intraoperative femur PPFs include revision THA, noncemented fixation, impaction
grafting, and compromised bone stock.3 The same patient risk factors that apply to
acetabular PPFs also apply to femoral PPFs1,3,4,6 (Table 1). Femur morphology also plays
a role in risk assessment; capacious Dorr type C femurs have a lower cortical-to-
cancellous bone ratio and may be associated with a 2- to 5-fold higher risk of
intraoperative PPF4 (Resource 1).


Etiology
Intraoperative acetabulum and femur fractures can occur at several points during THA.
Each distinct phase of the procedure is associated with unique risks, of which the
surgeon must be mindful. During initial dislocation, the femur undergoes its highest
torsional stress and is at greater risk for fracture than the acetabulum. To prevent
further compromise of the structural integrity of the bone during conversion from
previous hardware placement, the hip is dislocated before hardware removal,.
Acetabular reaming is associated with a lower fracture risk; however, a risk of over-
reaming the walls or floor (medial wall) exists. Trialing acetabular components or placing
final components into the acetabulum is associated with the risk of fracture occurring
with impaction. Broaching the femur is associated with calcar fractures and greater
trochanter fractures. Femoral reaming is associated with the risk of over-reaming of the
canal, leading to propagating fractures, whereas calcar planing may increase the risk of
calcar fractures.
If the surgeon is placing acetabular or femoral implants, reamers, or trials, the surgical
technique should be optimized while using mallets. Applying regular and steady force,
listening for pitch change, and evaluating the progress of trials or final implants are
critical to prevent intraoperative fractures.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Detection at time of surgery is vital to prevent the risks of revision surgery
Postoperative pain deep in the groin, instability, and persistent pain all are key findings

Patient History

The detection of intraoperative PPFs at the time of surgery is vital so immediate
treatment can be provided and to prevent future surgical and anesthetic risk to the
patient during revision surgery. If these intraoperative fractures go undetected at the
time of surgery, patients often present to the clinic postoperatively reporting thigh or
groin pain. Distinguishing this pain from postsurgical pain is important, which may make
diagnosis more challenging. Questions about instability, the location of the pain, pain
with weight bearing, pain with range of motion, persistent pain postoperatively, and
deep pain all are necessary questions to ask the patient to determine the source of pain.
Physical Examination
Acetabulum is more difficult to visualize
Sudden changes in tightness or audible cracks are signs
Assess for fractures along the walls, circumference, and protrusion.
Femoral fractures are more common, especially during final broaches in press-fit stems
Listen for pitch changes.
Broach and trial under direct visualization.
Acetabulum

Acetabulum
Intraoperatively, reaming in a stepwise manner and evaluation for osteophytes and the
true acetabulum are important. Osteophytes can be removed before or after acetabular
component placement; however, they should be removed to reduce the risk of
impingement that may lead to acetabular fracture. The timing of osteophyte removal
varies based on surgeon preference; however, landmarks may be lost if removal is
performed before reaming, and the acetabular component may become loose if already
in place. A well-secured acetabular component should move in continuity with the pelvis
if trialing using a grasper or handle. In addition, the acetabulum should not give in.
Assessment along the circumference of the acetabulum for fracture lines or evaluation
to determine if the acetabular component gives in medially is important.

Femur

Femur
The femur is at greatest risk for PPFs during final broaching and placement of the final
implant. Familiarity with the shape and contour of the implant and limited variability in
stem selection are critical to reduce user error, resulting in fractures. Consistent and
constant pressure when striking the handle is vital and allows for the observation of
pitch that provides the classic auditory indication of the implant being appropriately
seated. Care should be taken to visualize the calcar and evaluate the femur for fractures
throughout reaming, broaching, and final implant placement. In addition, during the
removal of broaches, the implant-specific design should be assessed for placement and
removal techniques to avoid damaging the greater trochanter. Finally, surgeons should
exercise care during dislocation and relocation of the hip because twisting motions of
the femur may lead to intraoperative fractures. A classic sign of an occult or non-
visualized fracture is the ability to continually sink broaches lower than the neck
resection or the previously noted level at which the broach engaged. Surgeons should
maintain vigilance, especially if larger broaches than indicated by the template are
necessary to achieve stability.
Imaging Studies
Intraoperative fluoroscopy and plain radiographs are the most common imaging studies
obtained.
At least two views always should be obtained.
AP pelvis, lateral hip/femur, and Judet views are useful.
Advanced imaging, such as CT and MRI, may be performed postoperatively if the initial
fracture was missed.

Imaging Studies

Intraoperative fractures can be confirmed via intraoperative fluoroscopy if available. If
not available, single-exposure radiographs are a good substitute. Similar to all fractures,
more than one view is ideal for making clinical decisions. In patients with an acetabular
fracture, AP pelvis, Judet, and lateral views are useful. In addition, component and pelvic
stability should be assessed via stress radiographs of the implant and pelvis. For a PPF of
the femur, AP, lateral, and oblique views should be adequate if the surgical field has not
been exposed to the suspected level of injury. Fractures commonly are nondisplaced or
minimally displaced and easily may be missed on fluoroscopic images and radiographs.
If the fracture is not identified at the time of surgery, postoperative plain radiographs
can be obtained. Additional advanced three-dimensional imaging, such as CT and MRI,
also can be used for treatment planning.
Classification and Management
Acetabular Fracture Classification

Acetabular Fracture Classification
The Paprosky classification of periprosthetic acetabulum fractures describes
management based on fracture patterns and deficiencies of the acetabulum.1,3 The
classification system can be used to guide treatment decision making in the surgical
setting3,7 (Table 2); however, the Paprosky classification system is complex and difficult
to implement clinically. Peterson et al8 classified acetabular fractures more simply as
stable or unstable acetabular cups regardless of fracture pattern.

Femoral Fracture Classification

Femoral Fracture Classification
The Vancouver classification of periprosthetic femur fractures remains the most
common classification of intraoperative periprosthetic fractures. This classification
system should not be confused with the Vancouver postoperative periprosthetic femur
fracture classification system because the two systems vary, in characteristics and
treatment options. Both classification systems are based on the location and type of
fracture1,3,9 (Table 3; Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4).

Principles of Periprosthetic Fracture Management
Not substantially different from the principles of any other fracture
Need to prevent stress risers and bypass fracture
Need to ensure that the construct and the fracture are stable

Principles of Periprosthetic Fracture Management
The principles of fracture management in patients with an intraoperative PPF do not
change substantially in the presence of an implant. The goal is to create a stable
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Periprosthetic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000508
14/28

construct capable of compression across the fracture site. Femoral intraoperative PPFs
often are managed first, after which the stem is inserted. If the fracture is stable, then no
management is necessary. If the fracture is nondisplaced, then the fracture can be
managed with the use of a cerclage wire to prevent fracture propagation, after which the
primary THA femur implant is inserted. For more distal fractures, the first step is to
bypass the fracture with the use of a stem that is longer than the distal end of the
fracture by at least two cortical diameters to provide enough distal fixation for the
stem.10 If the fracture is stable and the construct is long enough, then no additional
augments are necessary. If the fracture is unstable, then plates in combination with
cerclage wires, screws, or strut allograft can be placed to stabilize the fracture.
Initial Management
Assess the fracture pattern and its extent.
Identify the etiology of the fracture.
Management should be based on fracture type and implant stability.

Initial Management
The first step in the management of an intraoperative fracture is to stop and assess the
situation. Removal of the implant often is tempting; however, removal may not be the
best course of action. Instead, the surgeon should ask an assistant to hold the implant in
place while assessing the fracture and its stability. The surgeon must determine if the
implant is in an appropriate location and version. In addition, the surgeon must
determine if the implant is stable and if the fracture is displaced or comminuted. This
information is critical in deciding the next steps in management.
Nonsurgical Management
The construct must be stable.
The fracture pattern must be stable and not propagate.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM

The patient must be able to follow weight-bearing and activity restrictions.

Nonsurgical Management
In the nonsurgical management of intraoperative fractures, the implants must be stable
and the bone quality must be capable of bearing weight and muscular forces after the
implementation of a nonsurgical treatment plan. After ensuring that the construct is
stable and adequate bone stock is present, partial–weight bearing or toe-touch weight
bearing are acceptable; however, if pursuing non–weight-bearing options, the origins
and insertions of the muscles used to keep the hip in flexion or rotation must be
recalled. Depending on the fracture location, keeping the leg lifted in a non–weight-
bearing position may place additional stress across the fracture.
Surgical Management
Stabilize the fracture.
Restore biomechanics of the hip.
Produce a stable hip joint with appropriate leg lengths.
Management varies based on fracture pattern and bone involved.

Surgical Management
The goal of the intraoperative management of iatrogenic fractures is to ensure a stable
construct that allows for bone healing and results in a functional limb. For periprosthetic
fractures, the surgeon must consider prosthesis placement and design in making the
final decision about the implant construct and the fracture fixation plan. The surgeon
must consider alignment and stability of the hip joint and the stability of the fracture.
The acetabulum and femur should be considered independently, following separate
decision-making algorithms (Resource 2).

9/3/26, 4:31 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000508

Acetabular Fractures
Difficult bony anatomy and exposure
Assess the degree of displacement, stability of the construct, and version of the construct.
If the implant and pelvis are unstable, stabilize the pelvis first.
If only the implant is unstable, consider implant modification.

Acetabular Fractures
Acetabular fractures pose specific challenges because the acetabulum is comprised of
three irregularly shaped bones. Initial management requires assessment of the implant
and pelvis. If the pelvis, acetabulum, and implant are appropriately aligned and stable,
modified–weight bearing is a potential course of management; however, if the implant,
pelvis, or acetabulum are no longer stable, additional surgical management is required.
First, the anterior and posterior columns must be assessed for fractures that may lead to
instability. If the columns are largely intact, a larger primary acetabular component
(jumbo cup) with multiplanar screws may suffice as a treatment option. If the posterior
column is unstable or mild pelvic discontinuity is present, treatment options include
open reduction and internal fixation of the posterior column to stabilize the pelvis,
revision of the acetabular component (increased screw holes and thicker component
construct), or placement of a cup-cage construct. If pelvic discontinuity is grossly
unstable or if attempts at open reduction and internal fixation are inadequate, a cup-
cage or cage construct may be an appropriate treatment option. The decision-making
algorithm for intraoperative acetabulum fractures is shown in Figure 5.3,11

Femoral Fractures
Fracture stability and implant stability must be achieved.
Avoid stress risers over the implants or at the end of plates.
Cerclage wires or plates commonly are placed for proximal fractures; however, nerves and
vessels are at risk.

Femoral Fractures
Femoral fracture management largely follows the basic fracture principles of (1) avoiding
two constructs with a short distance of bone between them (kissing constructs), which
forms a stress riser, and (2) having at least two cortical diameters of distal fixation to the
fracture.10 For example, if the cortical diameter of the femur is 30 mm in the diaphysis, a
lateral plate or strut should overlap the implant and travel distal to the fracture by at
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Periprosthetic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000508
18/28

least 60 mm. Proximally, the plate should run as long as possible (Figure 6). A revision
THA femoral stem that extends past the distal end of the fracture by at least two cortical
diameters also may be inserted. Cerclage wiring for reduction often requires removal of
the press-fit stem, wiring, and replacement of the stem to prevent fracture propagation.
The location of the cerclage wires depends on the fracture type; however, care should be
taken to note adjacent nerves and vessels that may be caught in the cerclage wires. If a
fracture is observed along the calcar, a cerclage wire should be placed at the level of the
fracture and an additional wire should be placed distal to the fracture by two to three
cortical diameters to prevent fracture propagation.10 Intermittent placement of cerclage
wires between the fracture site and the distal cable is based on the surgeon preference
because 2 to 4 cm often are available between each wire. Cement should be avoided in
managing fractures because it may prevent healing if it enters the fracture site. Fractures
of the greater trochanter are best managed with the use of a claw plate or wires.

Outcomes
Data on acetabular fracture outcomes are relatively poor; however, but higher rates of implant
loosening and revision surgery have been noted.
Femoral fractures vary by fracture type and the ability to restore a stable construct and
fracture.
Greater trochanteric fractures are associated with good outcomes if the soft tissues remain
intact.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:31 PM
AAOS | Intraoperative Periprosthetic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000508
20/28

Fractures that can be bypassed by a stem typically result in good outcomes
Complications

Complications
Complications of intraoperative fractures include increased blood loss, extended
incisions, and increased surgical time, which is associated with an increased risk of
infection.12 In addition, postoperative patient expectations must be discussed because
primary THA is no longer straightforward. Discharge planning may need to be altered to
involve additional home support or rehabilitation placement.
Acetabulum

Acetabulum
Acetabular intraoperative PPFs are rare, and large reliable studies currently are
unavailable. Most acetabular fractures are occult or nondisplaced and are recognized as
a source of pain in the early postoperative period.11 Prospective studies are necessary to
fully determine the true outcomes of this complication. In larger intraoperative
acetabulum PPFs that require more invasive management, patients suffer from high
rates of implant loosening and revision.13,14
Femur

Femur
Intraoperative femur fracture outcomes vary based on fracture type, management, and
location. Multiple larger retrospective studies have found calcar fractures to result in
good bony union if managed with the use of cerclage wires.15,16 These studies have

found that cerclage wires ultimately result in satisfactory initial implant stability without
compromising clinical outcome measures.17 Greater trochanteric fractures generally
result in good outcomes, and recent research by Pritchett et al18 concluded that, unless
the construct is unstable or substantial fracture displacement is observed, fixation is not
required; however, failure to manage a greater trochanteric fracture that is unstable may
result in an antalgic gait because of loss of the abductors.18 Diaphyseal fractures
managed with the use of longer stems that bypass the fracture are associated with a
stem survival rate similar to that of primary THA but with lower Harris hip scores and
lower patient satisfaction.14 Delayed mobilization, weight-bearing restrictions, abductor
muscle impairment, and poorer improvements in functional outcomes contribute to the
lower scores.14

Posterior Approach
Most common approach
Easily extensile
Major complication is instability

Posterior Approach
Historically, the posterior approach has been the main approach for THA. If an
intraoperative fracture occurs, it is easily managed via an extensile approach. The
approach can be extended distally to the knee and proximally to expose the acetabulum.
Postoperative instability remains a major complication associated with the posterior
approach; however, appropriate prosthesis replacement, the use of a dual mobility
prosthesis, and good soft-tissue repair may minimize this risk.

Lateral Approach
The lateral approach to the hip results in a very stable hip construct but is associated
with the risks of abductor injury and heterotopic ossification. Similar to the posterior
approach, the lateral approach can be extended for the management of femoral and
acetabular fractures. It can be incorporated into a more posterior approach for
acetabular fracture management; however, care must be taken to not injure the
abductors further or damage the superior gluteal nerve.

Traditionally associated with the highest rate of femoral intraoperative PPFs

Direct Anterior Approach
The direct anterior hip approach has been associated with more femoral fractures than
the posterior and lateral approaches.19 In addition, extending the approach for surgical
management of a femur fracture may be a challenge given the locations of the nerves.
Therefore, the surgeon must understand the extensile approach. The lazy–S-shaped
incision allows for distal extension via an incision through the iliotibial track and
dissection laterally to allow for exposure of the vastus lateralis20 (Figure 8). The femoral
diaphysis can then be accessed via incision of the vastus fascia at the posterior border of
the femoral diaphysis. By making the incision at the greater trochanter, a muscular
bridge between the vastus and the medial gluteal muscles can be left intact while
mobilizing the vastus.21 The greater trochanter is placed at specific risk. Initial belief that
the anterior approach was associated with superior stability compared with the
posterior approach also has been questioned.19

Pearls
Press-fit implants are associated with a higher risk for intraoperative PPFs than cemented
implants.
Cerclage wires likely will be used to manage intraoperative femur fractures. The surgeon must
achieve good surgical exposure to prevent nerve and vessel injury by capturing these
structures with the use of a cerclage wire.
Patients with intraoperative PPFs have poorer outcomes compared with those who undergo
standard THA; however, PPFs that are identified and managed appropriately are manageable
complications.
Implant stability and fracture location determine the management of intraoperative PPFs.
